messages.content: How far will a car travel in time 't' when launched with velocity 'v' at an angle 'theta'?

function.name: calculate_projectile_range
function.description: Calculate the range of a projectile launched at an angle with initial velocity, using the kinematic equation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

initial_velocity.description: The initial velocity at which projectile is launched. This is a float type value.

angle.description: The angle at which projectile is launched. This should be in degrees. This is a float type value.

time.description: The time in seconds after which the range is to be calculated. This is a float type value.

message.content:
**Short answer**

If you only care about how far the car moves *horizontally* during a given time \(t\), the distance is simply

\[
x(t)=v\,\cos\theta \; t .
\]

If you want the *total distance travelled along the trajectory* (the length of the curve the car follows) you need both the horizontal and vertical components:

\[
\begin{aligned}
x(t)&=v\,\cos\theta \; t,\\[4pt]
y(t)&=v\,\sin\theta \; t-\tfrac12 g\,t^{2},\\[4pt]
s(t)&=\sqrt{x(t)^{2}+y(t)^{2}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### Why the simple formula works

- **Horizontal motion** is unaffected by gravity (ignoring air resistance).  
  The horizontal component of the initial velocity is \(v_x=v\cos\theta\).  
  Since horizontal acceleration is zero, the horizontal position grows linearly with time: \(x=v_x t\).

- **Vertical motion** is affected by gravity.  
  The vertical component of the initial velocity is \(v_y=v\sin\theta\).  
  The vertical position is \(y=v_y t-\tfrac12 g t^{2}\).

- The **total path length** up to time \(t\) is the Euclidean norm of the horizontal and vertical displacements.

---

### If you’re interested in the *range* (horizontal distance until the car lands)

Set the vertical displacement to zero again (i.e., \(y(t_{\text{flight}})=0\)):

\[
t_{\text{flight}}=\frac{2v\sin\theta}{g}.
\]

Plugging this into the horizontal distance gives the classic range formula:

\[
R=\frac{v^{2}\sin(2\theta)}{g}.
\]

---

### Quick reference

| Quantity | Formula | Notes |
|----------|---------|-------|
| Horizontal distance after time \(t\) | \(x=v\cos\theta\,t\) | No gravity effect |
| Vertical position after time \(t\) | \(y=v\sin\theta\,t-\tfrac12 g t^{2}\) | Gravity pulls down |
| Total path length after time \(t\) | \(s=\sqrt{(v\cos\theta\,t)^{2}+(v\sin\theta\,t-\tfrac12 g t^{2})^{2}}\) | Length of the curve |
| Range (horizontal distance until landing) | \(R=\dfrac{v^{2}\sin(2\theta)}{g}\) | Set \(y=0\) again |

Feel free to plug in your numbers (remember to convert \(\theta\) to radians if you’re using a calculator that expects radians). If you need help with a specific example or want to include air resistance, just let me know!
